rationale: The BOOK ENTRY's distinctive core (shadow of death as the world's patterned way of sin/darkness/bondage ending at the grave, structured as the opposite of a 'shadow of Christ' consisting of appointed times/assemblies/humbled way) is a synthetic construct that the cited texts and chapter method do not carry better than the ordinary reading. The primary passages depict a condition or locale of deep gloom, bondage, or deathly peril from which God delivers by presence or light; they do not define a dual symbolic 'Way' system or equate the phrase with the patterned substance of the world. Linking Rom 6:23 and Phil 2:5-9 supplies the wages/gift and humility motifs but does not establish that those motifs are what 'shadow of death' itself means. The chapter's broader claim that shadow = protective outline helps explain why the phrase is not ultimate death, yet still leaves the entry's world-way and oppositional apparatus as unsupported extras. The common reading accounts for the same verses with fewer steps and no contradiction to pastoral or prophetic usage.
book_core_identification: The shadow of death is the symbolic Way/pattern of the world shaped like Death's substance (sin, darkness, and bondage whose wages end at the pit or grave), opposite the shadow of Christ.
book_secondary_elaborations: Opposite: the Shadow of Christ (the appointed times, assemblies, and humbled Way shaped like His substance which leads through death to the gift of eternal life)
unsupported_glossary_assertions: It is the symbolic Way and pattern of the world shaped like Death's substance
That substance is specifically sin, darkness, and bondage whose wages end at the pit or grave
It stands as the structured opposite of the shadow of Christ (appointed times, assemblies, and humbled Way)
chapter_only_objections: Global redefinition of every 'shadow' as protective shelter/outline rather than gloom (including the Colossians 2 and Hebrews 10 readings of the law's feasts)
Claim that the feasts remain a present shadow of still-future good things and are therefore the shadow of Christ
Heaven-and-hell chapter's denial of intermediate conscious states and endless torment as the backdrop for 'pit or grave'
Extension of tselem/tsel image-theology so that every shadow necessarily implies a lit body casting an outline of substance
strongest_counter_interpretation: In the dominant biblical and Christian usage, 'the shadow of death' (tsalmaveth / skia thanatou) is poetic imagery for the deepest darkness, gloom, or mortal peril associated with the threat or nearness of death (or, in the prophetic/NT strand, the spiritual darkness and hopelessness of those without God), a condition or valley through which God may accompany and from which He delivers by light or presence; it is not a technical label for the world's sinful way-system opposite Christ's appointed times.
counter_core_identification: Extreme death-associated darkness/gloom or mortal/spiritual peril (traversed under divine protection or dispelled by messianic light).
material_core_denial: The phrase does not name or function as the world's patterned way of sin/bondage structured as the opposite of Christ's shadow of appointed times; it remains situational imagery of deathly darkness or danger.
counter_case: Psalm 23:4 presents a valley the shepherd's rod and staff comfort the speaker while traversing; this fits lived mortal peril far more directly than 'walking the world's sinful pattern.'

Psalm 107:10, 14 and Isaiah 9:2 / Luke 1:79 describe people sitting/dwelling in darkness and the shadow of death who are then brought out or illuminated; the grammar is locative/conditional, not definitional of a cosmic Way.

Job's repeated uses (though not printed with the entry) treat the phrase as the land or gates of deep gloom associated with death itself, reinforcing the ordinary sense against a unique 'world-pattern' reading.
Romans 6:23 and Philippians 2:5-9 supply general death/life and humility motifs but never employ the phrase 'shadow of death,' so they cannot redefine it.
The traditional reading requires no extra system of paired opposite shadows and matches both the Septuagint/Vulgate tradition that shaped the NT citations and ordinary pastoral use.
book_explanatory_advantages: Consistent gathering of 'shadow' uses can highlight protective or outline senses that soften pure-gloom readings
Explicit pairing with light/morning texts (Amos 5:8, Isa 9:2, Ps 107) shows the phrase is not ultimate annihilation
Rom 6:23 supplies a clean wages/gift contrast that can be laid beside the deliverance texts
counter_explanatory_advantages: Fits the actual syntax and pastoral force of Psalm 23:4 without converting the valley into the entire world-system
Accounts for the bondage and dwelling language of Ps 107 and Isa 9 / Luke 1 as a condition rather than a named Way
Requires no unstated equation between 'shadow of death' and 'shadow of Christ' or importation of Colossians feast theology into the glossary entry
Aligns with the full range of poetic uses (Job, Jeremiah, Amos) as deathly gloom rather than a single dualistic pattern
Explains why the NT simply re-uses the Isaiah phrasing for messianic illumination without erecting an opposite-shadow architecture
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Psalm 23:4's explicit comfort by rod and staff while the speaker walks the valley (the shepherd leads in righteous paths, then through peril, not through 'the world's sinful way' as such)
The locative phrasing 'valley of / land of / sit in the shadow of death' across the cited texts, which describes a place or state of gloom rather than defining the patterned substance of the world
unresolved_objections: The precise etymology of tsalmaveth (death-shadow compound vs. deep-darkness) remains debated, though either lexical option still favors ordinary gloom/peril over the entry's world-way construct
